entities.name: Mirim Çelebi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mirim Çelebi (died 1525), an eminent Ottoman astronomer and mathematician, represented the intellectual zenith of Islamic astronomical traditions in the early 16th century, bridging the sophisticated observational and computational techniques developed at the Maragha and Samarkand observatories with the burgeoning scientific interests of the Ottoman Empire. His work, particularly his commentaries on Ulugh Beg's *Zij-i Sultani*, established him as a pivotal figure in the transmission and perpetuation of advanced celestial mechanics and trigonometry from Central Asian Islamic scholarship into the Ottoman scientific milieu. Born into a lineage of distinguished scholars—his grandfather was Qadi Zadeh al-Rumi and his father was Ali Qushji, both towering figures in Timurid astronomy—Çelebi inherited and meticulously built upon a rich intellectual legacy that emphasized precise astronomical tables and theoretical critiques of Ptolemaic models.

Çelebi's primary contribution was his comprehensive commentary, *Sharh al-Mulakhkhas fi al-Hay'a*, on al-Jagmini's astronomical treatise, and more significantly, his *Sharh-i Zij-i Ulugh Beg* (Commentary on Ulugh Beg's Star Catalogue). This latter work, completed around 1500, meticulously explained and expanded upon the intricate mathematical and observational methodologies of Ulugh Beg's monumental *Zij-i Sultani*, which was compiled at the Samarkand Observatory in the 1420s. Çelebi's commentary not only elucidated the complex trigonometric calculations and planetary models but also offered critical insights into the instruments and observational practices employed by Ulugh Beg's team. His work served as a crucial pedagogical text, widely studied in madrasas across the Ottoman realm, thereby solidifying the Samarkand school's influence on subsequent Ottoman astronomy.

entities.summary:
Mirim Çelebi (1401, Samarkand – 1525), born Mahmud ibn Muhammad, was a towering figure in 16th-century Ottoman astronomy and mathematics, whose intellectual lineage directly traced back to the illustrious Samarkand school. As the grandson of both the renowned astronomer and mathematician Qadi Zada al-Rumi and the Timurid polymath Ulugh Beg, Çelebi inherited a profound scientific legacy, becoming a critical conduit for the transmission of advanced Central Asian astronomical knowledge to the Ottoman Empire. His life spanned a period of intellectual flourishing and strategic expansion for the Ottomans, under sultans Bayezid II and Selim I, who actively patronized scientific endeavors and sought to integrate the intellectual traditions of their newly acquired territories.

Çelebi's most significant contribution was his seminal treatise, *Dastūr al-ʿAmal fī Taqwīm al-Aflāk* (Manual for the Almanac of the Spheres), completed around 1500. This comprehensive work served as an essential commentary and revision of Ulugh Beg's monumental *Zij-i Sultani*, the most accurate star catalog and astronomical tables of its time. Çelebi meticulously updated and expanded upon his grandfather's work, providing detailed explanations, new calculations, and practical applications for celestial observation and calendar construction. His methodology often involved sophisticated geometrical and trigonometrical techniques, showcasing the advanced state of Islamic mathematical astronomy.
